Yes—Election Day should be a national holiday. Right now, millions of Americans are effectively prevented from voting by work and school schedules, not by a lack of civic interest. Making Election Day a paid holiday would remove those scheduling barriers and make participation easier and more inclusive.

It also reframes voting as something worth showing up for—a civic celebration rather than a chore squeezed between obligations. That matters for democracy itself.

Support is broad: 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans back this measure. And internationally, it’s not an unusual idea—27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, suggesting this approach is compatible with functioning election systems.

Making Election Day a national holiday sounds helpful, but by itself it won’t reliably solve the barriers that keep people—especially low-income workers—from voting.

First, Election Day as a federal holiday doesn’t guarantee paid time off from private employers. Federal holidays apply to federal workers and may not require private businesses (especially retail, restaurants, caregiving, gig-adjacent jobs) to close or give employees extra paid leave. In practice, the very workers most likely to miss voting because of inflexible schedules are the ones least likely to benefit from a holiday policy.

Second, even where some workplaces close, low-wage workers are often still required to work essential shifts. A holiday can reduce the inconvenience for some people, but it can leave others in the same situation—meaning turnout gains are uncertain.

Third, the key reforms are those that directly change voting access rules, not general workplace calendars. State-level policies that require job-protected time to vote (or paid leave policies), plus practical measures like automatic voter registration and better early/absentee options, target the bottleneck more directly. Those approaches can be designed to apply uniformly to employers rather than relying on voluntary compliance or the assumption that businesses will treat a holiday the same way.

Finally, the “evidence” that other democracies do elections on holidays doesn’t show that a holiday *by itself* increases turnout. Even in countries that schedule elections on weekends/holidays, turnout depends on the whole package of voting access, early voting rules, ID requirements, registration systems, and enforcement. In the U.S., focusing on a holiday alone risks overpromising while not addressing the real day-to-day constraints.

So, I oppose a national Election Day holiday and support more reliable, enforceable voting-access reforms—like guaranteed time to vote and automatic voter registration—because they directly reduce barriers for the people least able to absorb schedule disruptions.
